# Richard Stallman: Key Information
Richard Stallman is an American computer programmer and activist, born in 1953 in New York City. He studied physics at Harvard University, and became involved with the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory as a programmer in 1971, where he participated actively in the hacker culture and contributed to various projects such as TECO and Emacs. Stallman became known for his opposition to restricted computer access and his advocacy for user freedom.
Stallman is best known for founding the GNU project in 1983, with the aim of creating a free Unix-compatible operating system. He also founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 and promoted the concept of copyleft, introducing the GNU General Public License (GPL). Stallman contributed essential tools such as GCC and GNU Emacs, and advocated for naming the combined GNU system and Linux kernel as "GNU/Linux." His activism extends to campaigns against DRM, software patents, and proprietary software, along with ongoing public talks and writings on software freedom. Stallman has been a central and sometimes controversial figure in free software communities, influencing terminology, culture, and political stances around technology. As of 2021, he has returned to the FSF board of directors despite controversy regarding his public statements and social conduct.
